blocks.title: Why RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks. The learner's job is not to memorize RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved unsupported claim rate per answer.

Running case: faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson assumes you can learn the vocabulary, then spends its effort on integration choices, failure signals, and checks that make the idea usable in a real system.

items.text: Product framing: RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure unsupported claim rate per answer on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks

spans.text: Scenario: A RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks. The team wants to improve unsupported claim rate per answer, but it has already seen this failure: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Question: "Can I get a refund after 35 days if I lost my invoice?" The answer must cite the exact policy chunk, not a plausible refund rule remembered by the model.

Artifact: faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. It specifies loaders, chunk metadata, retriever settings, prompt contract, citation format, and a faithfulness check for unsupported claim rate per answer.
Worked output: retrieve policy-refunds-v3 section 4, quote "30 days" and "invoice id required", answer that the request probably fails the policy, and link the source chunk used.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: RAG reviewer. Context: A RAG answer sounds fluent but may include claims not supported by retrieved chunks. Task: inspect faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks. Require a user question, retrieved chunks with source ids, final answer, and a claim-by-claim support check. Constraints: do not allow claims that are absent from retrieved chunks; flag stale or missing metadata. Output: {question, retrieved_sources, answer, unsupported_claims, release_decision}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the mechanism in the running case

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means separating retrieval quality from answer quality: did the system fetch the right evidence, and did the model stay faithful to that evidence?
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to faithfulness evaluation rubric with claim-level support checks: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: unsupported claim rate per answer becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful RAG Evaluation and Faithfulness design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: Retrieved chunks mention the right keyword but not the answer-bearing paragraph.
The answer is relevant but unfaithful: it adds a policy or fact not present in the retrieved evidence.
Metadata is missing, so citations cannot be checked or reranked later.
The broad warning sign: unsupported claim rate per answer gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.useWhen: Use the production path when unsupported claim rate per answer affects users, trust, safety, cost, or compliance.
blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: the answer is relevant to the question but adds facts outside the evidence.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Make the failure visible before making the system more sophisticated.
